message.reasoning:
The user asks "is vs code running". They want to check if VS Code is running. We can use the cmd_controller_execute tool to run a command that checks if VS Code process is running. On Windows, we can use tasklist or powershell. Let's use tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq Code.exe" and parse output. But the tool just executes command; we can't parse output. But we can run a command that returns something like exit code? Actually tasklist will return output but we cannot capture it. However we can run a batch script that writes to a file or echo something. But the tool only returns whatever the command outputs. So we can run a command that prints "VS Code is running" or "not running" based on existence of process. We can write a small batch file that uses tasklist and then echoes accordingly.

We can create a .bat file content:

@echo off
tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq Code.exe" | findstr /I "Code.exe" >nul
if %ERRORLEVEL%==0 (
    echo VS Code is running
) else (
    echo VS Code is not running
)

Then execute that bat file. But we need to create the file first. We can use cmd to create file via echo > file. Or we can embed the entire script into a single command using parentheses and redirection. For example:

cmd /c "(echo @echo off>check_vs_code.bat & echo tasklist /FI \"IMAGENAME eq Code.exe\" ^| findstr /I \"Code.exe\" >nul>>check_vs_code.bat & echo if %%ERRORLEVEL%%==0 (>>check_vs_code.bat & echo     echo VS Code is running)>>check_vs_code.bat & echo ) else (>>check_vs_code.bat & echo     echo VS Code is not running)>>check_vs_code.bat & echo )>>check_vs_code.bat) && check_vs_code.bat"

But that's messy. Alternatively, we can directly run a one-liner that checks and echoes. For example:

cmd /c "tasklist /FI \"IMAGENAME eq Code.exe\" | findstr /I \"Code.exe\" >nul && echo VS Code is running || echo VS Code is not running"

This will print either message. That might suffice. So we can call cmd_controller_execute with that command.
